EmoReward: Self-Evolving Reward Calibration for Emotional Video Generation RL

Mingzhe Zheng Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Yue Wu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Jing Tan Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Chang Zou Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Dengyang Jiang    Zeyue Tian    Xuanhua He    Ryan Xu Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Yunyang Ge Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Sihui Ji Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Yunlong Lin Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Kaihang Pan Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Hongru Yan Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Sixiang Chen Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Dianyi Wang    Julian Zhang Affiliation: Fudan University University of Waterloo    Weijie Kong Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Changlin Li Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Lanqing Guo Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Zhao Zhong Affiliation: The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology Tencent Hunyuan    Qifeng Chen    Harry Yang    *Work done during internship at Tencent Hunyuan
Project leader  Corresponding author
Abstract

Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has advanced generative model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, but evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Existing approaches typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that poorly capture emotional intent and can invite reward hacking, while reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is difficult to scale and subject to individual aesthetic differences that complicate the calibration of facial, body motion, and chromatic cues across narrative contexts. We introduce EmoReward, a new self-evolving training mechanism that distills evidence reliability from reward traces collected during an actual training run to adaptively guide multi-reward weight allocation in subsequent training by determining which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. EmoReward first plans specific grounding cues from the emotional prompt to guide evaluation, then uses heterogeneous signal primitives to score the generated video during the act stage. Reflective Reward Gating calibrates their contributions through instance-level gates for phase, face confidence, conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over the active set to produce the sample’s fused reward. RewardMemory then estimates each primitive’s reliability from rollout scores and outcomes within each emotional regime in the finished training run, then fixes bounded multipliers that calibrate fusion weights in the next training run without updating reward models. Experiments on HunyuanVideo 1.5 show improvements across multiple RL algorithms and compare EmoReward with other agentic reward methods under SAGE-GRPO. Ablations and transfer experiments on SD 3.5 and FLUX further support adaptive reward calibration for visual generation.

Project Page: https://emoreward-project.github.io/

GitHub Repo: https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/EmoReward

1  Introduction

Reinforcement learning (RL), especially Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), has advanced model post-training in verifiable domains such as code and mathematics, where correctness provides a direct learning signal [46, 16, 50, 75]. In contrast, evaluating video quality, especially emotional expression, often depends on subjective aesthetics and has no uniquely correct target. Visual post-training adapts diffusion and flow generators through RL and preference objectives [2, 12, 43, 60, 72, 29, 80]. Learned evaluators provide scores for image preference and video quality [69, 22, 38, 68, 17, 30], but a visually clear, temporally stable video can match its prompt without conveying the intended emotion. Facial analysis, dynamic expression recognition, and multimodal emotion models supply complementary evidence [1, 3, 7, 26, 79], whose reliability varies with context: facial cues require visible faces, strong motion can undermine restrained sadness, and saturated colors may reflect style rather than emotional intent. This raises a central question: Which emotional evidence should the reward system trust in the current video, and how can it adaptively determine how much weight to assign to that evidence?

Agentic systems coordinate interaction, refine outputs through feedback, and organize evaluation into rubrics [65, 62, 39, 47, 15]. These capabilities motivate adaptive evaluation, yet existing video GRPO methods typically rely on fixed rewards for visual quality, motion quality, and text alignment that inadequately capture emotional intent. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and preference optimization address subjective goals [8, 48, 41, 44], but human annotation is costly at scale, and aesthetic differences complicate the calibration of emotional cues across contexts. Fixed fusion can mix informative, missing, and saturated signals, allowing policy updates to exploit scoring shortcuts rather than improve emotional fidelity. This motivates reward calibration at two complementary levels: assessing which cues are valid within each video, and learning from a completed training run how much those cues should influence rewards in the next run.

We introduce EmoReward, a self-evolving training mechanism for emotional video-generation RL (Figure 1). It distills evidence reliability from reward–outcome traces collected during an actual, completed training run, then uses this experience to guide multi-reward weight allocation in the next run to decide which emotional evidence to trust and how much to weight it. Plan translates emotional intent into an EmoScript specifying affect targets, facial and body cues, and an expression window; Act scores generated videos with heterogeneous primitives, keeping criterion scores separate from evidence validity. Within each video, Reflective Reward Gating calibrates these cues using the training phase, face confidence, semantic conflict, and subtlety, then renormalizes weights over active providers. After a training run, RewardMemory estimates provider reliability for each emotional regime from traces. Providers with stronger agreement are given larger weight multipliers for the next run, with limits on the size of the adjustment. These multipliers and all reward models stay fixed throughout that run; for each new video, reflection further downweights or excludes missing or unsuitable cues before the active scores are combined into a weighted average EmoReward can be integrated into several RL algorithms alongside general video rewards, and directly use training experience to calibrate reward allocation without retraining the evaluators.

We evaluate EmoReward on HunyuanVideo 1.5 [64] with DanceGRPO [72], FlowGRPO [29], and SAGE-GRPO [80], observing higher VideoAlign scores for the guided configurations across all three RL algorithms on emotional prompts as the evaluation dataset for rollout. Under a fair comparison on the same RL architecture and training budget, EmoReward achieves the highest reliability selectivity and both composite calibration scores among seven reward policies. Ablation studies and mechanism analyses examine the contributions of reflective gating, provider pools, and RewardMemory (Section 4.2). Transfer experiments on Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX show gains in selected configurations alongside objective-dependent trade-offs, while user studies show that EmoReward receives the highest human preference and proportion of Good ratings and the lowest proportion of Bad ratings for emotional fidelity, temporal coherence, and visual quality.

Our contributions are threefold.

  • •

    We introduce EmoReward, to our knowledge the first self-evolving training mechanism for emotional video generation RL that calibrates reward providers across training runs without updating reward model parameters.

  • •

    We propose RewardMemory, to our knowledge the first memory designed for multi-reward systems in video generation. It distills evidence reliability into bounded fusion weights, enabling iterative calibration of RL reward signals across training runs.

  • •

    We inspire a novel cross-run self-evolution paradigm for post-training multimodal foundation models: a completed training run informs reward allocation in the next, making training experience reusable at the run level. Extensive experiments across three video RL algorithms and two image backbones, with ablations and human evaluations, validate EmoReward’s effectiveness.

2  Related Work

From verifiable RL to agentic feedback for non-verifiable rewards.

RLHF learns subjective preferences [8, 41], whereas verifiable RL exploits correctness checks [16, 75]. Agentic evaluators [77, 9] and adaptive rubrics [15, 70, 78] structure open-ended feedback. Related approaches route experts [40], refine responses [39], evolve rewards [35, 76], or organize experience [47, 71]. JitRL derives closed-form policy updates from retrieved action advantages [25]. EmoReward instead transfers reward–outcome evidence across completed training runs to calibrate frozen providers, combining sample-level gating with persistent fusion weights.

Agents for visual content creation.

Agentic visual creation organizes generation into planning, tool use, and feedback-driven refinement. Video agents coordinate multi-shot narratives, script evaluation, audiovisual planning, and learned camera control[82, 18, 81, 11, 57, 67]. Image agents combine knowledge retrieval [14, 4], learned creation and editing policies [23, 27], and experience reuse [5, 6]. Other approaches jointly improve generation and evaluation [28, 51]. EmoReward naturally achieves a self-evolving mechanism in video generation RL training, rather than building a workflow or retraining reward models.

RLHF for visual generation and the emotion-reward gap.

Visual reward models capture preferences and multidimensional quality [69, 22, 66, 38, 68, 63, 30]. Optimization using rewards and preferences extends from images [2, 12, 43, 60] to video and flow models [72, 29, 80, 31], with benchmarks assessing quality and compositional alignment [20, 32, 49]. Related 3D, audiovisual, and objectives for human animation address complementary aspects of visual generation [24, 19, 59, 55]. Motion editing and transfer [52, 54, 37], shape-aware and consistent image editing [33, 36], and pose- and identity-preserving animation [58, 42, 56] offer finer control over visual content. Distillation [74, 21, 13] and feature reuse [34] improve generation efficiency, complementing reward-based post-training. Affect-grounded augmentation [61] and reflective action-conditioned generation [73] further connect feedback with video synthesis. Temporal video modeling and dynamic facial-expression recognition provide additional perceptual foundations [53, 3]. Emotion understanding supplies multimodal evidence [7, 26, 79] and grounded affect representations [45, 10, 1]; EmoReward addresses how their reliability should govern reward fusion across scenes and training runs.

3  Method

3.1  Preliminaries

Multi-reward optimization with GRPO.

Let pp be a prompt and xx a generated video from a policy πθ​(x∣p)\pi_{\theta}(x\mid p); a scalar reward is R⁡(x,p)∈ℝR(x,p)\in\mathbb{R}. For a prompt pp, GRPO samples a group 𝒢⁡(p)={xi}i=1G\mathcal{G}(p)=\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G} and forms standardized group advantages

Ai=R⁡(xi,p)−μ𝒢σ𝒢+ϵ,μ𝒢=1G​∑jR⁡(xj,p),σ𝒢2=1G​∑j(R⁡(xj,p)−μ𝒢)2,A_{i}=\frac{R(x_{i},p)-\mu_{\mathcal{G}}}{\sigma_{\mathcal{G}}+\epsilon},\qquad\mu_{\mathcal{G}}=\tfrac{1}{G}\textstyle\sum_{j}R(x_{j},p),\quad\sigma_{\mathcal{G}}^{2}=\tfrac{1}{G}\textstyle\sum_{j}(R(x_{j},p)-\mu_{\mathcal{G}})^{2}, (1)

which enter the clipped, KL-regularized objective in Appendix F. The policy update depends on reward differences inside the group. A common additive constant cancels exactly; positive rescaling changes only the relative effect of ϵ\epsilon. A coefficient of variation measures dispersion, not policy-learning signal quality; we also assess within-prompt ranking agreement and downstream quality.

Why static emotion fusion fails.

Given reward primitives 𝒯={1,…,K}\mathcal{T}=\{1,\ldots,K\} with normalized scores sk​(x,p)∈[0,1]s_{k}(x,p)\in[0,1], a fixed fusion is Remostatic=∑kwk0​skR_{\mathrm{emo}}^{\mathrm{static}}=\sum_{k}w_{k}^{0}s_{k} with wk0≥0,∑kwk0=1w_{k}^{0}\geq 0,\sum_{k}w_{k}^{0}=1. This assumes a fixed trust allocation across scenes, although facial visibility and the relevance of motion depend on the intended emotion. Writing each primitive as a constant plus a group-varying part sk=ck+δks_{k}=c_{k}+\delta_{k} and splitting into an active set 𝒜\mathcal{A} and a dead/saturated set 𝒟\mathcal{D},

Remostatic=∑k∈𝒜wk0​δk+∑k∈𝒜wk0​ck+∑k∈𝒟wk0​ck,R_{\mathrm{emo}}^{\mathrm{static}}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}}w_{k}^{0}\delta_{k}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}}w_{k}^{0}c_{k}+\sum_{k\in\mathcal{D}}w_{k}^{0}c_{k}, (2)

the constant terms cancel from the centered GRPO numerator. Removing them alone need not change the standardized advantage. Calibration matters when provider validity, errors, or relative contributions vary across candidates, or when the emotion branch is mixed with another reward. EmoReward addresses these cases through gates and memory-conditioned fusion.

3.2  Overview

EmoReward grounds emotional intent, scores visual evidence, and calibrates provider trust:

p→Plane⁡(p),(x,e)→Act{sk,uk},(s,u,e,x)→ReflectRemo,ℳ→EvolvewRM​(z).p\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Plan}}e(p),\quad(x,e)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Act}}\{s_{k},u_{k}\},\quad(s,u,e,x)\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Reflect}}R_{\mathrm{emo}},\quad\mathcal{M}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Evolve}}w^{\mathrm{RM}}(z). (3)

Here e⁡(p)e(p) is an EmoScript, uku_{k} denotes evidence validity, and zz is the emotional-context signature. RewardMemory ℳ\mathcal{M} stores completed reference-run traces; Evolve produces wRM​(z)w^{\mathrm{RM}}(z) and exports the corresponding regime multipliers mk​(r)m_{k}(r) (Section 3.5). Reflect combines these fixed multipliers with current-video gates. The resulting emotion reward is mixed with a general video reward:

Rtotal​(x,p)=α​Rvid​(x,p)+β​Remo​(x,p)α+β,R_{\mathrm{total}}(x,p)=\frac{\alpha R_{\mathrm{vid}}(x,p)+\beta R_{\mathrm{emo}}(x,p)}{\alpha+\beta}, (4)

where RvidR_{\mathrm{vid}} is the evaluation score supplied by the original reward system, for example a general video-quality evaluator [30]; α,β≥0\alpha,\beta\geq 0 control its mixture with the calibrated emotion reward, with α+β>0\alpha+\beta>0. Figure 2 connects these stages through their shared fusion interface.

3.3  Plan and Act: Emotional Grounding

Plan: prompt-conditioned criteria.

The planner converts the prompt into an EmoScript independently of RewardMemory:

e⁡(p)=(v⋆,a⋆,𝐪AU⋆,𝐛⋆,Ω).e(p)=(v^{\star},a^{\star},\mathbf{q}^{\star}_{\mathrm{AU}},\mathbf{b}^{\star},\Omega). (5)

The implemented representation contains scalar valence and arousal targets, target facial AU intensities, body cues, and an expression window. The memory regime is inferred later from observed context. Continuous VAD trajectories and dominance targets are outside this implementation. The EmoScript separates intended affect from its observable cues. For example, restrained sadness need not imply large motion or an exaggerated face: target intensities, body cues, and the expression window define what to assess, while reliability is determined from the generated evidence and completed-run experience.

Act: observation and scoring.

Act evaluates a video already sampled from πθ(⋅∣p)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid p); it does not generate or revise the video. Each provider returns

(sk,uk)=𝒮k​(x,e⁡(p)),sk,uk∈[0,1],(s_{k},u_{k})=\mathcal{S}_{k}(x,e(p)),\qquad s_{k},u_{k}\in[0,1], (6)

where 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} is provider kk’s scoring operator, which aggregates frame-level measurements or evaluates the whole clip. The seven fusion providers comprise a VLM judge, facial AUs, body cues, temporal evidence, CLIP-AUTT, R1-Omni, and motion naturalness; chromatic atmosphere and kinetic intensity are auxiliary readouts, giving nine observation channels. Score sks_{k} measures criterion agreement, while uku_{k} marks usable evidence. A missing face channel’s neutral default is not evidence and is excluded through its validity mask. Auxiliary readouts do not enter the seven-provider calibration policy. Appendix C specifies scoring interfaces; Figure 5 illustrates the toolkit studied in Section 4.2.

3.4  Reflect: Instance-Level Calibration

Reflect computes provider-specific gates from the current evidence, prompt, and training step. The factorization is

gk=gkphase​gkconflict​gkface​gksubtle​uk,gk∈[0,1],g_{k}=g^{\mathrm{phase}}_{k}\,g^{\mathrm{conflict}}_{k}\,g^{\mathrm{face}}_{k}\,g^{\mathrm{subtle}}_{k}\,u_{k},\qquad g_{k}\in[0,1], (7)

with neutral factors for channels to which a condition does not apply. Phase denotes the training-step warmup, face gating controls face-dependent evidence, conflict gating attenuates disagreement between semantic providers, and subtlety gating restrains intensity-sensitive cues. Motion naturalness uses its observation confidence. These controls are computed, not learned (Appendix D).

Evidence-dependent trust.

The phase factor schedules reward evidence over generator training, distinct from the within-video expression window. Face gating limits channels requiring facial evidence; conflict and subtlety gating temper disagreeing semantic assessments and intensity-sensitive cues. Their provider-specific application changes relative influence; a shared positive attenuation would largely cancel under normalization.

Composition with experience.

For a fixed base weight wk0w_{k}^{0}, define the effective contribution ak​(x,p)=wk0​gk​(x,p)​mk​(r⁡(x,p))a_{k}(x,p)=w_{k}^{0}g_{k}(x,p)m_{k}(r(x,p)). Reflective Reward Gating uses mk=1m_{k}=1; EmoReward uses the fixed table produced by Evolve. With 𝒜={k:ak>ϵg}\mathcal{A}=\{k:a_{k}>\epsilon_{g}\}, active-provider normalization gives

Remo​(x,p)=∑k∈𝒜ak​(x,p)​sk​(x,p)∑k∈𝒜ak​(x,p)+ϵ.R_{\mathrm{emo}}(x,p)=\frac{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}}a_{k}(x,p)s_{k}(x,p)}{\sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}}a_{k}(x,p)+\epsilon}. (8)

Invalid evidence receives no mass. A common positive factor cancels except through the stabilizer; calibration acts through relative provider contributions and differences between videos. Regime rr selects a table entry; gate gkg_{k} controls current evidence validity. A provider favored by memory still contributes nothing when its current evidence is invalid. With no memory entry, unit multipliers recover Reflect-only fusion; the scoring interfaces and generator objective remain the same.

3.5  Evolve: RewardMemory

RewardMemory treats reward allocation as a decision over emotional context zz: the providers are actions, their fusion weights form a policy, and a stored outcome yy supplies a non-parametric reliability signal. Experience is collected during a completed reference training run with Reflective Reward Gating. Each trace mi=(zi,{sik},{gik},wi,Ri,yi)m_{i}=(z_{i},\{s_{i}^{k}\},\{g_{i}^{k}\},w_{i},R_{i},y_{i}) records context, scores, gates, weights, and outcomes. Evolve groups these traces into a regime neighborhood 𝒩⁡(z)\mathcal{N}(z), with a global fallback for insufficient support, and computes

ρk​(z)=Covi∈𝒩⁡(z)⁡(sik,yi)σsk​σy+ϵ,Akrel​(z)=ρk​(z)−1K​∑jρj​(z).\rho_{k}(z)=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}_{i\in\mathcal{N}(z)}(s_{i}^{k},y_{i})}{\sigma_{s^{k}}\sigma_{y}+\epsilon},\qquad A_{k}^{\mathrm{rel}}(z)=\rho_{k}(z)-\frac{1}{K}\sum_{j}\rho_{j}(z). (9)

Reliability uses raw provider scores; constant scores receive zero correlation. It measures agreement with the reference outcome, not independent emotional fidelity. The centered advantage tilts the base allocation through bounded multipliers:

Δk=clip⁡(Akrel/τ,−c,c),wkRM​(z)=wk0​eΔk∑jwj0​eΔj.\Delta_{k}=\operatorname{clip}(A_{k}^{\mathrm{rel}}/\tau,-c,c),\qquad w_{k}^{\mathrm{RM}}(z)=\frac{w_{k}^{0}e^{\Delta_{k}}}{\sum_{j}w_{j}^{0}e^{\Delta_{j}}}. (10)

This is the closed-form optimum of a KL-regularized allocation with clipped utilities (Appendix F). The exported mk​(r)=eΔkm_{k}(r)=e^{\Delta_{k}} compose with current instance gates in Eq. 8. The table is fixed throughout the next training run: only the generator receives gradient updates, and runtime lookup neither re-estimates reliability nor writes back to the table. Algorithms 1 and 2 separate reward computation from between-run memory construction. Appendix E explains context grouping and table construction; Appendix I provides a trace-based worked example.

4  Experiments

Experimental settings.

We use HunyuanVideo 1.5 with DanceGRPO, FlowGRPO, and SAGE-GRPO, fusion α=β=0.5\alpha=\beta=0.5, batch size 22, and group size G=4G=4. The updated optimizer comparison reports average results on a subset of 302 emotional prompts that does not overlap with the training set. GT denotes the pretrained generator without RL. Each guided row uses one fixed configuration: Reflect for DanceGRPO, and the complete EmoReward system for FlowGRPO and SAGE-GRPO. The controlled seven-policy comparison retains its separate step-100 evaluation protocol. VideoAlign supplies RvidR_{\mathrm{vid}} and the reference outcome yy. Memory calibration uses K=7K=7, τ=0.5\tau=0.5, a log-multiplier cap c=1c=1, and minimum context support nmin=20n_{\min}=20. Appendix J.1 gives the qualitative protocol.

Evaluation metrics.

Table 1 reports mean ±\pm SEM across prompts for VideoAlign Overall, visual quality (VQ), motion quality (MQ), text alignment (TA), PickScore, and CLIPScore. The latter two are frame-averaged preference and alignment proxies; their exported logits are scaled by 2626 and 3030, respectively. VideoAlign is also an optimization objective, so agreement with it is distinguished from independent emotional fidelity.

4.1  EmoReward as a Base-RL-Agnostic Reward Add-on

Table 1 compares the pretrained reference, each optimizer baseline, and its fixed guided configuration. All four VideoAlign heads increase for every RL algorithm under the fair comparison experimental settings. Overall improves by 0.32180.3218 for DanceGRPO with Reflect, 0.23430.2343 for FlowGRPO with EmoReward, and 0.56450.5645 for SAGE-GRPO with EmoReward. The reference comparison and within-optimizer comparison answer different questions: the former evaluates the full post-training system, while the latter compares reward configurations. PickScore and CLIPScore show smaller, mixed changes; the VideoAlign gains do not imply uniform improvement on all evaluation axes.

Emotion-category analysis.

Figure 5 compares GT and SAGE-GRPO with EmoReward across six metrics and eight emotion categories. The four VideoAlign heads improve in every category, while PickScore and CLIPScore show smaller, nonuniform changes. This GT comparison reflects the complete post-training system. Categories overlap within the evaluated set.

4.2  Ablations and Mechanism Analysis

Agentic reward methods.

Our controlled study fixes the backbone and optimization budget and varies the reward policy across seven arms: VideoAlign-only, single-provider, random, round-robin, fixed fusion, Reflective Reward Gating, and RewardMemory.

Reward-policy ablation.

Table 2 compares relative reward dispersion, reliability selectivity, and normalized Emotion-Gating Benchmark (EGB) pillars. Adding RewardMemory yields the highest selectivity (0.4280.428) and both composite scores (core 0.9220.922, emo 0.8840.884); the variant without memory leads the standalone preference pillar. SNR∗ is a dispersion statistic, not a measure of gradient quality. The composites combine an ImageReward preference proxy, dispersion, and agreement-weighted selectivity; Appendix G defines their scope.

Reward-provider pool.

Figure 5 compares a VideoAlign baseline, semantic emotion cues, motion naturalness, and a balanced pool. Weights and curricula also differ, so this study motivates the interface rather than isolating each channel’s causal effect (Appendix H). Seven channels enter memory calibration; chromatic and kinetic readouts remain auxiliary.

Memory-conditioned trust.

Macro and motion receive the largest global multipliers (1.8331.833, 1.5101.510), whereas three constant channels receive 0.7780.778. Memory reallocates trust but cannot activate invalid evidence. Macro shares evaluator information with the reference outcome, so its correlation reflects objective agreement. Appendix E describes context-specific allocation; Appendix I illustrates its arithmetic on real rollout scores. A matched global-memory control remains necessary to isolate the benefit of contextual calibration.

4.3  Generalization to image backbones

Image transfer covers SD3.5 and FLUX with three optimizers. Results are objective-dependent: SD3.5–DanceGRPO improves on HPSv3 with calibration, whereas FLUX’s HPSv3-optimized baseline remains strongest on that metric. Unequal SD3.5 training budgets limit causal attribution. Appendix J details the settings and full-prompt comparisons.

4.4  Human evaluation

Eighteen participants rated the three methods on 30 prompts using Bad/Normal/Good for emotion fidelity, temporal coherence, and visual quality. Table 3 shows that EmoReward obtains the highest Good shares (60.0%60.0\%, 54.3%54.3\%, 57.2%57.2\%), compared with 53.0%53.0\%, 51.5%51.5\%, and 45.0%45.0\% for SAGE-GRPO, and the lowest Bad shares on all three criteria. These descriptive results complement the automatic metrics; aggregation and statistical scope are detailed in Appendix B.

The complete distributions reveal a distinction that Good shares alone obscure: SAGE-GRPO also receives more Bad ratings than GT on every criterion. EmoReward lowers Bad shares relative to both comparison groups while increasing Good shares. This pattern supports examining the entire ordinal distribution, rather than reducing it to a binary preference. The reported margins do not resolve variation across people or prompts; participant- and prompt-level records are required for uncertainty estimates that account for repeated judgments.

5  Conclusion

In this paper, we proposed EmoReward, a self-evolving reward calibration framework for emotional video generation reinforcement learning. EmoReward combines instance-level Reflective Reward Gating with RewardMemory, which transfers provider-reliability estimates from a completed training run to subsequent optimization without updating reward-model parameters. Experiments across video optimizers, complemented by ablations, image-transfer analyses, and human ratings, support the utility of adaptive calibration while identifying objective-dependent trade-offs. These findings suggest that completed-run experience can inform the allocation of trust among heterogeneous reward providers, providing a foundation for further research on reward-system evolution across training.

Reproducibility Statement

The appendix specifies the reward interface, calibration rule, mathematical derivation, evaluation protocol, complete comparison tables, and qualitative examples. Source artifacts include editable figures and scripts for constructing tables and visualizations.

AI Use Statement

AI assistance was used for manuscript editing, mathematical checks, and figure preparation. The authors are responsible for verifying the scientific claims and final submission. Experimental comparison images and video frames were taken from the evaluated models; no additional media were synthesized to illustrate experimental outcomes.

Appendix A Limitations and Future Work

Beyond emotional video generation.

EmoReward studies a training-adaptive reward system that transfers evidence about provider reliability between generator-training runs without updating reward-model parameters. The present evaluation focuses on emotion, where different scenes call for different combinations of facial, gestural, semantic, and motion evidence. A broader application would require a task-appropriate provider pool and a meaningful outcome for calibration. Action fidelity and audio–visual correspondence are natural visual extensions; language models and tool-use agents could similarly combine semantic judges, execution checks, and trajectory-level assessments. Whether the same calibration rule transfers effectively remains an empirical question, especially when providers share errors or outcomes favor only part of the task.

Iterative evolution across training runs.

A completed training run can be treated as a unit of experience for its successor. Repeating this procedure could produce a sequence of generators and reward-allocation tables, with each generation contributing new traces. Our experiments evaluate a reference-to-calibrated transition, not sustained improvement across many generations. Such an extension must address distribution shift, stale evidence, and feedback loops that reinforce a proxy’s errors. Retaining diverse historical traces and evaluating held-out outcomes would be important tests of whether repeated calibration remains useful.

Model-level human feedback.

The trace representation also suggests a way to carry human assessments of a completed model into subsequent training. For example, a reviewer who finds movement too weak could request greater emphasis on suitable motion providers in the affected contexts; excessive motion could motivate the opposite adjustment. This would complement sample-level preference feedback with structured assessments of a model’s final behavior, translated into bounded changes to the next run’s reward allocation. Mapping subjective feedback to providers and regimes, reconciling different raters, and preventing compensating failures remain open design questions. The ordinal study reported here evaluates outputs; it does not implement this proposed feedback mechanism.

Appendix B Human Evaluation: Ordinal Ratings

Study and comparison groups.

The study includes 18 participants and 30 prompts, with one video per prompt from each of three methods: the pretrained generator without RL (GT), SAGE-GRPO, and SAGE-GRPO with EmoReward. GT is a generator baseline, not a ground-truth human video. Participants assessed each output separately on three criteria using Bad, Normal, or Good. The supplied aggregate results contain 540 judgments for each method–criterion combination, consistent with the full participant–prompt product. Across all three methods and criteria, there are 4,860 categorical judgments. These ordinal counts are separate from the earlier pairwise preference protocol; pairwise choices are not converted into categorical ratings.

Criteria.

Emotion fidelity concerns how convincingly the video conveys the prompt’s intended affect, including whether expression and gesture fit its emotional tone. Temporal coherence concerns continuity of expression, identity, and movement through the clip. Visual quality concerns perceptual detail, anatomy, and visible artifacts. The categories distinguish poor, intermediate, and good quality on each axis. They are rated separately rather than collapsed into a single preference or an assumption that stronger emotional intensity is always better.

Aggregation and rounding.

For method mm, criterion cc, and rating category bb, the percentage is:

p^m,c,b=100​Nm,c,b∑b′∈{Bad,Normal,Good}Nm,c,b′,∑b′Nm,c,b′=540.\widehat{p}_{m,c,b}=100\,\frac{N_{m,c,b}}{\sum_{b^{\prime}\in\{\mathrm{Bad,Normal,Good}\}}N_{m,c,b^{\prime}}},\qquad\sum_{b^{\prime}}N_{m,c,b^{\prime}}=540. (11)

Table 3 rounds each percentage independently to one decimal place and bolds only the highest Good percentage within each criterion. Rounding may make a three-category total differ from 100.0%100.0\% by 0.10.1 percentage points. The raw integer counts are preserved in the accompanying source data, rather than rounded before normalization. All nine aggregate blocks have the stated denominator; the totals alone do not establish participant-level completeness or the absence of duplicate records.

Reading the distributions.

Relative to SAGE-GRPO, EmoReward’s Good share increases by 7.07.0, 2.82.8, and 12.212.2 percentage points for emotion fidelity, temporal coherence, and visual quality, respectively. These differences are computed from the unrounded counts. Its Bad share falls from 31.5%31.5\% to 15.4%15.4\% for emotion fidelity, from 28.9%28.9\% to 20.2%20.2\% for temporal coherence, and from 30.9%30.9\% to 15.9%15.9\% for visual quality. The complete distribution matters: compared with GT, SAGE-GRPO has more Good ratings but also more Bad ratings on every criterion, so a Good-only summary would omit part of the observed pattern.

Statistical scope.

The present report uses the supplied aggregated counts. It does not treat repeated judgments from the same participant or prompt as independent observations. Participant- and prompt-level records are needed for uncertainty estimates that respect both sources of dependence; no confidence interval or significance claim is inferred from the aggregate margins. The aggregates do not document recruitment, presentation order, blinding, exclusions, or prompt-selection provenance. Those collection details must be established from the study records rather than inferred from the rating totals.

C.7  Score normalization and validity

The evaluated fusion consumes the providers’ bounded scores directly. An optional running-statistic normalization is not an additional transformation applied to those scores. Availability and confidence are retained separately from score magnitude: unavailable evidence receives a neutral fallback but zero effective contribution. Motion confidence is incorporated once through its channel gate, while an activity mask handles unavailable motion observations. This convention avoids counting the same confidence twice. The micro, body, and temporal channels are constant in the analyzed reference traces; their neutral readings do not establish the absence of visible faces or bodies in the generated videos.

Reflect separates training progress, semantic consistency, observation availability, and the prompt’s intended intensity. A factor is neutral for providers to which it does not apply. Let tt denote the generator update, s0<s1s_{0}<s_{1} the phase-transition endpoints, γmin\gamma_{\min} a phase floor, and qfq_{f} the available face-evidence ratio:

The semantic-conflict factor attenuates disagreement d=|sCLIP​-​AUTT−sR1​-​Omni|d=|s_{\mathrm{CLIP\text{-}AUTT}}-s_{\mathrm{R1\text{-}Omni}}| above a threshold θd\theta_{d}, with lower bound γd\gamma_{d}. Implementation settings.

In our implementation, the default warmup endpoints are s0=40s_{0}=40 and s1=100s_{1}=100, with γmin=0.1\gamma_{\min}=0.1. Face gating uses θf=0.35\theta_{f}=0.35; semantic conflict uses θd=0.20\theta_{d}=0.20 and γd=0.35\gamma_{d}=0.35. For subtle prompts, detected using θa=0.4\theta_{a}=0.4 or prompt cues, (ξf,ξt,ξe)=(0.85,0.75,0.80)(\xi_{f},\xi_{t},\xi_{e})=(0.85,0.75,0.80); the motion floor is λg=0.55\lambda_{g}=0.55. These are rule-based controls rather than learned reward-model parameters. Historical exported traces retain their recorded gates; the default specification alone does not reconstruct a past run’s full configuration.

Effect on normalized fusion.

A factor shared by every active provider cannot by itself redistribute trust. For gk=γ​hkg_{k}=\gamma h_{k} with γ>0\gamma>0, active normalization yields

Remo=∑kwk​hk​sk∑kwk​hk+ϵ/γ.R_{\mathrm{emo}}=\frac{\sum_{k}w_{k}h_{k}s_{k}}{\sum_{k}w_{k}h_{k}+\epsilon/\gamma}. (26)

Except for the stabilizer, the common scale cancels. Reflect changes the relative allocation through provider-specific factors, invalidation, and composition with the original reward branch. The face-activity proxy used to group exported traces in Appendix E is distinct from the current video’s face-evidence ratio.

Appendix E Evolve: RewardMemory Construction and Use

Record the reference run (Figure 7A).

A completed run with Reflective Reward Gating supplies the experience used by RewardMemory. Each trace keeps the prompt–video context, raw provider scores, gates, applied weights, and VideoAlign outcome separate. The context describes target affect and available evidence; its face-activity proxy records whether selected scoring branches depart from their neutral defaults, rather than measuring visible-face coverage. The recorded scores and outcomes provide the basis for comparing providers.

Build the calibration table (Figure 7B).

The complete reference bank is grouped by target arousal and face-branch activity, with a global fallback for contexts with insufficient support. Within each group, reliability is the correlation between a provider’s raw scores and VideoAlign outcomes, before gating. Algorithm 2 compares each provider with the group’s average reliability and converts the difference into a capped weight multiplier (Eq. 10). This calibrates reward allocation without fitting a value network or changing any reward model.

Use the memory in the next run (Figure 7C).

Algorithm 1 looks up the matching multipliers, combines them with the base weights and current-video gates, and normalizes over active providers. Memory sets the allocation from prior experience; reflection can still suppress unavailable or unsuitable cues. The table remains fixed throughout generator training. Panel C illustrates this multiply-and-normalize step using recorded scores and illustrative starting weights: it is a controlled replay, not an additional training run. Reflect-only fusion omits the memory adjustment; Appendix I explains the worked example.

Appendix F Derivation of the Closed-Form KL Update

For positive base weights on the supported simplex, consider

max⁡∑kw∈ΔK−1⁡wk​Akrel−τ​∑kwk​log⁡wkwk0.\max_{w\in\Delta^{K-1}}\sum_{k}w_{k}A_{k}^{\mathrm{rel}}-\tau\sum_{k}w_{k}\log\frac{w_{k}}{w_{k}^{0}}. (27)

The Lagrangian has stationary condition Akrel−τ⁡(log⁡(wk/wk0)+1)+λ=0A_{k}^{\mathrm{rel}}-\tau(\log(w_{k}/w_{k}^{0})+1)+\lambda=0. Normalizing the resulting exponentials gives wk=wk0​eAkrel/τ/∑jwj0​eAjrel/τw_{k}=w_{k}^{0}e^{A_{k}^{\mathrm{rel}}/\tau}/\sum_{j}w_{j}^{0}e^{A_{j}^{\mathrm{rel}}/\tau}. Strict concavity yields a unique optimum. A shared additive baseline in the utilities cancels from this unclipped solution.

For Δk=clip⁡(Akrel/τ,−c,c)\Delta_{k}=\operatorname{clip}(A_{k}^{\mathrm{rel}}/\tau,-c,c), the same derivation applies to clipped utilities A~k=τ​Δk\widetilde{A}_{k}=\tau\Delta_{k}. Since e−c≤∑jwj0​eΔj≤ece^{-c}\leq\sum_{j}w_{j}^{0}e^{\Delta_{j}}\leq e^{c}, normalized weights satisfy

e−2​c≤wkRMwk0≤e2​c.e^{-2c}\leq\frac{w_{k}^{\mathrm{RM}}}{w_{k}^{0}}\leq e^{2c}. (28)

The cap bounds relative changes; it does not guarantee a one-hot distribution as τ→0\tau\to 0. Zero base weights remain outside the support.

Scope of the bound and cold start.

The interval [e−c,ec][e^{-c},e^{c}] bounds the exported, unnormalized multipliers; the normalized weight ratio has the wider bound above. Clipping the utilities is not equivalent to solving the original objective subject to a prescribed hard KL constraint. If all advantages are zero, the update returns w0w^{0}. A constant provider has ρk=0\rho_{k}=0, but its centered advantage is negative only when the mean reliability is positive; constant scores therefore do not imply unconditional down-weighting. In the supplied traces, positive-reliability providers make this relative attenuation observable. None of these algebraic properties proves improved generalization or emotional fidelity.

Group-relative invariance.

If Ri′=a​Ri+bR_{i}^{\prime}=aR_{i}+b with a>0a>0, then μ′=a​μ+b\mu^{\prime}=a\mu+b, σ′=a​σ\sigma^{\prime}=a\sigma, and

Ai′=Ri−μσ+ϵ/a.A_{i}^{\prime}=\frac{R_{i}-\mu}{\sigma+\epsilon/a}. (29)

Translation cancels exactly. By contrast, CV⁡(R)=σ/(|μ|+ϵ)\operatorname{CV}(R)=\sigma/(|\mu|+\epsilon) is not translation invariant. Consequently, a reward offset can increase relative dispersion without improving the standardized group advantage. This is an algebraic property, not an experimental claim about learning efficiency.

Generator Optimization Objective

For completeness, we state the clipped GRPO objective underlying the group advantages in Eq. 1 [46]. Let hi,th_{i,t} denote the generation state and ai,ta_{i,t} its sampled transition in candidate trajectory ii. Define ϱi,t​(θ)=πθ​(ai,t∣hi,t,p)/πθold​(ai,t∣hi,t,p)\varrho_{i,t}(\theta)=\pi_{\theta}(a_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t},p)/\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(a_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t},p). With clipping radius εclip\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}} and reference-policy regularization coefficient κ\kappa,

𝒥GRPO​(θ)=\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)={} 𝔼p,{xi}∼πθold[1G∑i=1G1Ti∑t=1Ti(min{ϱi,tAi,clip(ϱi,t,1−εclip,1+εclip)Ai}\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p,\{x_{i}\}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{T_{i}}\sum_{t=1}^{T_{i}}\left(\min\!\left\{\varrho_{i,t}A_{i},\operatorname{clip}(\varrho_{i,t},1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{clip}})A_{i}\right\}\right.\right. (30)
−κDKL(πθ(⋅∣hi,t,p)∥πref(⋅∣hi,t,p)))].\displaystyle\left.\left.-\kappa\,D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h_{i,t},p)\,\|\,\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid h_{i,t},p)\right)\right)\right].

Here TiT_{i} is the number of sampled transitions, πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} is the rollout policy, and πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} is a fixed reference policy. The scalar reward of the completed video determines AiA_{i}; advantages and reward-provider outputs are treated as constants during the policy update. This expression states the common clipped objective; individual video optimizers specify their transition likelihoods, sampled timesteps, and regularization. EmoReward changes the scalar reward supplied to the optimizer, not those optimizer-specific choices. Its generator KL penalty is distinct from the reward-allocation KL term derived above, whose variables are provider weights rather than generator parameters.

Appendix G Reward-Gating Metrics and Reproducibility

Table 2 reports two reward diagnostics (SNR∗ and Sel.), three normalized pillars (EF, GD, GR), and two composites (core, emo). All seven policies use the same backbone and optimization budget. The exported evaluation contains 160 four-candidate groups for VideoAlign, single-provider, and random routing, and 152 groups for each remaining policy. Thus the available sample counts differ, even though the nominal training budget is shared. The references identify scoring models or routing mechanisms, not reproductions of complete agentic systems.

G.1  Reward Diagnostics

Let RiR_{i} denote the fused training reward, yiy_{i} the VideoAlign reference outcome, and si,ks_{i,k} provider kk’s score. A group gg contains candidates for one prompt.

Reward–outcome agreement (ROA).

ROA is an auxiliary input to GR rather than a displayed column in Table 2. It measures within-group pairwise ranking agreement. For outcome-nontied pairs 𝒞g={(i,j):i⁡<j,|yi−yj|>​ϵy}\mathcal{C}_{g}=\{(i,j):i<j,\ |y_{i}-y_{j}|>\epsilon_{y}\}, the intended statistic is

Agr(g)=1|𝒞g|∑(i,j)∈𝒞g[𝟏{(Ri−Rj)(yi−yj)>0}+12𝟏{Ri=Rj}].\operatorname{Agr}(g)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}_{g}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{C}_{g}}\left[\mathbf{1}\{(R_{i}-R_{j})(y_{i}-y_{j})>0\}+\frac{1}{2}\mathbf{1}\{R_{i}=R_{j}\}\right]. (31)

The reported agreement is ROA=Meang⁡Agr⁡(g)\mathrm{ROA}=\operatorname{Mean}_{g}\operatorname{Agr}(g). The supplied pairwise helper uses ϵy=10−9\epsilon_{y}=10^{-9} and returns 1/21/2 when no outcome-nontied pairs exist. However, its treatment of reward ties differs from the symmetric half-credit convention above. The original aggregation script is unavailable; we therefore retain the archived ROA values as inputs to GR, without claiming to have recomputed their tie handling. VideoAlign-only obtains one by construction when its reward and reference ordering coincide. ROA measures agreement with that evaluator, not independent human or emotional quality.

Within-group relative dispersion (SNR∗).

With population standard deviation within each group,

Dg=Stdi∈g⁡(Ri)|Meani∈g⁡(Ri)|+ϵD,SNR∗=1|𝒢|​∑g∈𝒢Dg.D_{g}=\frac{\operatorname{Std}_{i\in g}(R_{i})}{|\operatorname{Mean}_{i\in g}(R_{i})|+\epsilon_{D}},\qquad\mathrm{SNR}^{*}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}|}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}D_{g}. (32)

The supplied diagnostic implementation uses ϵD=10−6\epsilon_{D}=10^{-6}. This is a coefficient of variation, not a signal-to-noise power ratio. A reward offset can increase it while leaving centered GRPO advantages unchanged; a high value neither establishes nor is necessary for better policy gradients. We report the archived per-policy reductions, separately from the aggregate-level checks below.

Reliability selectivity (Sel.).

Let ρk=Corr⁡(s⋅,k,y)\rho_{k}=\operatorname{Corr}(s_{\cdot,k},y) over the policy’s evaluated candidates, using the nine-channel diagnostic pool 𝒫\mathcal{P}. For Z=∑k∈𝒫|ρk|>0Z=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}}|\rho_{k}|>0,

qk=|ρk|Z,Sel.=1−−∑k∈𝒫qklogqklog⁡|𝒫|,0log0=0.q_{k}=\frac{|\rho_{k}|}{Z},\qquad\mathrm{Sel.}=1-\frac{-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{P}}q_{k}\log q_{k}}{\log|\mathcal{P}|},\qquad 0\log 0=0. (33)

The pool includes chromatic and kinetic readouts as well as the seven fusion providers. Sel. describes concentration of absolute provider–outcome correlations, not applied fusion weights. It discards correlation signs and does not establish causal provider usefulness. All seven reported policies have Z>0Z>0; the auxiliary zero-sample row and its all-zero-profile convention are excluded. Recomputing Sel. from the exported correlation profiles agrees with the stored values within 5×10−55\times 10^{-5}.

G.2  Normalized Pillars and Composite Scores

For the fixed comparison set 𝒜\mathcal{A} of seven policies, define

N⁡(va)=va−minb∈𝒜⁡vbmaxb∈𝒜⁡vb−minb∈𝒜⁡vb.N(v_{a})=\frac{v_{a}-\min_{b\in\mathcal{A}}v_{b}}{\max_{b\in\mathcal{A}}v_{b}-\min_{b\in\mathcal{A}}v_{b}}. (34)

The supplied reducer returns zero for a constant input across policies; none of the three reported inputs is constant. Normalization is specific to the compared set, so the resulting scores are not absolute measures transferable across benchmarks.

EF: preference-proxy pillar.

EFa=N⁡(Ia)\mathrm{EF}_{a}=N(I_{a}), where IaI_{a} is the archived mean ImageReward score [69]. EF retains the benchmark’s “Emotion Fidelity” abbreviation, but its input is a general visual preference model. We do not interpret it as an independent measurement of emotion fidelity. The raw means and normalization inputs are included in the supplement.

GD: relative-dispersion pillar.

GDa=N⁡(SNRa∗)\mathrm{GD}_{a}=N(\mathrm{SNR}^{*}_{a}). The benchmark calls this Gating Discriminativeness; mathematically, it is the normalized coefficient of variation above. Its inclusion does not turn reward dispersion into a gradient-quality measurement.

GR: agreement-weighted selectivity pillar.

GRa=N(Sel.aROAa)\mathrm{GR}_{a}=N(\mathrm{Sel.}_{a}\,\mathrm{ROA}_{a}). GR combines correlation-profile concentration with agreement with the reference evaluator. Both inputs are diagnostic summaries; the product does not establish an independent reliability ground truth.

core and emo: two specified aggregations.

The equal-weight composite and preference-emphasized composite are

corea=EFa+GDa+GRa3,emoa=λEF​EFa+λGD​GDa+λGR​GRa.\mathrm{core}_{a}=\frac{\mathrm{EF}_{a}+\mathrm{GD}_{a}+\mathrm{GR}_{a}}{3},\qquad\mathrm{emo}_{a}=\lambda_{\mathrm{EF}}\mathrm{EF}_{a}+\lambda_{\mathrm{GD}}\mathrm{GD}_{a}+\lambda_{\mathrm{GR}}\mathrm{GR}_{a}. (35)

Here the nonnegative coefficients sum to one; our implementation uses (λEF,λGD,λGR)=(0.5,0.25,0.25)(\lambda_{\mathrm{EF}},\lambda_{\mathrm{GD}},\lambda_{\mathrm{GR}})=(0.5,0.25,0.25). Full EmoReward scores 0.9220.922 on core and 0.8840.884 on emo, leading under both specified weightings. Reflect without memory leads EF. These observations concern the defined composites and comparison set, not arbitrary weightings or universal superiority.

Appendix H Extended Evaluation and Ablations

Provider-pool construction.

Figure 5 presents the main-text visual comparison; Table 5 quantifies the same four reward configurations used to construct the provider interface. Semantic emotion and motion cues improve some axes while exposing trade-offs on text alignment and preference. The configurations also differ in fusion weights and curricula; their comparison is not a single-factor ablation. In the semantic-cue configuration, the CLIP channel has zero fusion weight and cannot explain a training gain attributed to an active CLIP reward.

Ranking agreement.

For each four-candidate group, let 𝒞={(i,j):i<j,yi≠yj}\mathcal{C}=\{(i,j):i<j,\ y_{i}\neq y_{j}\}. We use

Agr(𝒢)=1|𝒞|∑(i,j)∈𝒞[𝕀{(Ri−Rj)(yi−yj)>0}+12𝕀{Ri=Rj}].\operatorname{Agr}(\mathcal{G})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{C}}\left[\mathbb{I}\{(R_{i}-R_{j})(y_{i}-y_{j})>0\}+\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbb{I}\{R_{i}=R_{j}\}\right]. (36)

Groups without comparable pairs are excluded. Agreement is averaged over groups; reward ties receive half credit independently of sample ordering. The analysis contains 160 baseline groups for DanceGRPO and 168 groups for each other optimizer–reward configuration, totaling 1,504 groups and 6,016 videos. These training candidates are separate from the 30-prompt fixed-checkpoint evaluation sets.

Memory sensitivity.

Across 27 temperature, neighborhood-size, and memory-window settings, the memory rule exceeds fixed weighting at the final window in 23 settings. None has a positive difference when averaged over all windows. These settings reuse the same traces and are not independent training seeds. The results motivate sensitivity analysis rather than a claim of monotonic improvement with accumulating memory.

Appendix I RewardMemory: A Worked Rollout Example

Figure 7 connects recorded provider scores, a previously exported calibration table, and a reproducible allocation calculation. Appendix E explains the principles behind panels A–C. The clips contain 81 frames at 24 fps and have 624×\times352 resolution; we display frames 12, 40, and 72. The four videos are candidates for one prompt from a reference rollout group. Their scores and outcomes come directly from the accompanying reward records; the images are decoded full frames. The macro provider has positive within-group outcome correlation, while three channels return their neutral constant. These four examples illustrate local behavior, not the population estimate used to construct RewardMemory.

Separating observations from the replay.

The exported table’s global entry differs from its context-specific entries. We use the global entry here to isolate the reweighting operation, without claiming that it was the entry selected for these historical videos. The initial active allocation is (0.336,0.440,0.134,0.090)(0.336,0.440,0.134,0.090) over macro, motion, CLIP-AUTT, and R1-Omni, with zero mass on the other three providers. These are illustrative starting weights, not reconstructed runtime gates. Multiplying by the exported global multipliers and renormalizing produces approximately (0.417,0.450,0.082,0.052)(0.417,0.450,0.082,0.052). On rollout #2’s recorded scores, the weighted mean changes from 0.5780.578 to 0.5630.563; its actual logged emotion reward is 0.7210.721. The distinction matters because the historical reward used its own training phase and configuration. An increase in a provider’s allocation need not increase the scalar fused score, and neither change alone establishes improved generated quality.

Prompt.

The camera slowly pushes forward, a cold side light slanting through the window frame, carving a sharp beam across the dimly lit study and illuminating the man seated at his desk. He leans slightly forward, hands folded over the keyboard, fingers tapping the keys with slow, precise rhythm. Shot from a low angle behind and to the side, the frame captures his furrowed brow and narrowed eyes, his gaze fixed like a needle on the flickering stream of code on the screen. His lips are pressed into a thin line, the jawline taut with concentration, nostrils fluttering faintly with each breath, occasionally biting his lower lip as if swallowing an unspoken question. The light casts a soft shadow across his forehead, making the sharp glint in his eyes even more intense. In the background, scattered papers and empty coffee cups rest silently on the bookshelf, while the rhythmic tapping of the keyboard echoes in the stillness, like the pulse of a heartbeat. He suddenly pauses, raises his right hand to his temple, his eyes briefly drifting, then swiftly refocuses on the screen—a quiet resolve, a steadfast defiance against time.

Appendix J Generalization to Image Generation

We evaluate Stable Diffusion 3.5 and FLUX with three optimizers and three reward configurations on 256 DrawBench prompts per checkpoint: 18 settings and 84 checkpoints. Internal Emo measures the emotion-stack reward; HPSv3 is a general preference objective also used to train the baseline. Neither independently measures perceived emotion.

SD3.5 baseline results average three checkpoints at 420–500 updates; calibrated variants average five at 2,780–3,000. FLUX baseline checkpoints span 2,760–3,000, and calibrated checkpoints 2,780–3,000. Standard errors describe checkpoint variation, not independent training seeds. Per-prompt arrays support the reported means; paired significance requires complete sample and generation-seed mappings and is not claimed.

Observed transfer pattern.

With SD3.5–DanceGRPO, HPSv3 rises from 9.5529.552 (baseline) to 10.09610.096 (Reflect) and 10.30210.302 (EmoReward). SD3.5–FlowGRPO declines on both HPSv3 and internal Emo; FLUX’s HPSv3-optimized baseline leads on HPSv3 across optimizers. Thus transfer is objective-dependent rather than uniformly beneficial.

J.1  Qualitative comparison protocol

Image plates use four curated prompts per displayed setting; video plates cover three optimizers. Figure 5 separately compares provider configurations. These examples illustrate behavior, not a randomly estimated win rate.

Images retain all original pixels. SD3.5 baseline outputs use 500 updates and calibrated outputs 3,000. The first two FLUX baseline cases use the only saved examples at 500 updates; all other FLUX rows use 3,000. Unequal budgets prevent attributing qualitative differences solely to calibration. Image seeds are unavailable, so only prompts are matched. Video rows share prompts and recorded sampling seeds. Clips are 864×\times480 at 24 fps; full frames at 0.5, 2.5, and 4.5 seconds are decoded without interpolation or retouching. The source bundle includes synchronized playback and editable figures.

The ordinal ratings in Appendix B complement these proxy-based and qualitative comparisons; raw participant/prompt records are needed to quantify uncertainty. The depicted scenes are generated content.
